question: 596. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the way in which incidents of gender-based violence (GBV) are recorded monitored and tracked across State agencies; if there is a centralised system for GBV data; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [69194/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Zero Tolerance, the Third National Strategy on Domestic, Sexual and Gender-based Violence (DSGBV), recognises the importance of collecting and monitoring data on gender-based violence; enhanced data collection and coordination is a key objective of the strategy. Cuan, our statutory agency dedicated to tackling DSGBV, is responsible for coordinating our national response and Government actions in the strategy, and a key part of their work is strengthening how data is gathered and used. Cuan has a dedicated research and data function responsible for collecting and analysing data across the DSGBV sector, to enable better monitoring and planning for services. Additional funding was made available to Cuan to expand the development of the national domestic violence helplines which also enables increased data collection. Government Departments, agencies and service providers gather and report data relevant to the implementation of the strategy to Cuan on key performance indicators to track and measure progress. For incidents of gender-based violence, An Garda Síochána have the lead role in recording details of such incidents in the PULSE system. I am advised that in July 2021, AGS introduced a mechanism to record the relationship between the victim and the offender. Since then, the Garda Information Service Centre (GISC) has implemented a data quality coherency check on the recording of the relationship, to improve the recording of the domestic abuse motive attached to PULSE incidents. This data coherency check was modified in June 2024. It now involves a review of all incidents in which the relationship between the victim and the offender has been recorded as falling into one of five categories (current intimate partner/spouse, former intimate partner/spouse, family member: parent/child, family member: sibling, or family member: other family member) but a domestic abuse motive has not been recorded. The domestic abuse motive is then added to incidents in instances where it is required. This improves the data gathered by AGS in relation to domestic violence. GISC routinely publish statistics in relation to these Data Quality Coherence Checks. With respect to the prevalence of gender-based violence in Ireland, the CSO conducted a Sexual Violence Survey; the results of which were published in 2023. The data gathered from that survey is used to inform policy and service provision. A further national survey is planned to take place in 2027. Cuan is represented on my Department's Analytics Steering Group and is engaging with the European Institute for Gender Equality (EIGE) on progressing aligned country data across EU member states. Early progress has been made on a Cuan/ESRI Joint Research Programme on Adult Sexual Violence in Ireland. This will include analysis of the 2023 CSO Sexual Violence Survey data, to examine patterns of victimisation among those that have experienced adult sexual violence and the profile of those that disclose experiencing adult sexual violence and use services. Alongside this, my Department is progressing work to develop a single unique identifier and standardising data categorisation across the Justice Sector which will facilitate better collation and sharing of data to support policy research and inform DSGBV service development.

question: 597. Deputy Cormac Devlin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his attention has been drawn to the case of a person (details supplied); if he will review the details of the case and provide an update on its current status; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [69197/25]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The naturalisation application referred to by the Deputy was refused by my Department. The person cited did not supply the requested documentation, therefore, the application was deemed ineligible and subsequently closed. It is open to the person cited to make a new application at any time. There is no time limit within which they can make a new application, nor is there any maximum limit on the number of applications. To maintain the integrity of the file on record, Citizenship Division do not return documentation submitted. However, should applicants wish to lodge a new application, they may request all relevant documents previously submitted to be associated with the new application. Citizenship Division have produced a guidance document for all potential applicants, outlining which documents are required for the application. This document is published on my Department's Irish Immigration website and is available here: www.irishimmigration.ie/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Citizenship-Guidance-Document-April-2024.pdf . Detailed information on how to apply for naturalisation and other resources is available here: www.irishimmigration.ie/how-to-become-a-citizen/. As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 598. Deputy Cormac Devlin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for a breakdown, by year, of the number of individuals removed from the State under the European Communities (Free Movement of Persons) Regulations 2015, which transpose the free movement directive; the reasons for removal in each case; the date on which each order was made and implemented; whether a ten-year ban was applied in each case; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [69208/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The removal of people who are involved in criminality and those who are a danger to society is a priority for me as Minister and my Department works closely with An Garda Síochána and the Irish Prison Service to ensure high risk persons are prioritised for removal from Ireland. I can advise the Deputy that on Monday 13 October 2025, removal orders were enforced against 23 Romanian citizens who were removed from Ireland by charter flight. These orders were made in accordance with the Free Movement Directive (Directive 2004/38/EC), on grounds of criminality and re-entry bans of up to 10 years have been applied to prevent their return to Ireland. Under the European Communities (Free Movement of Persons) Regulations 2015, which transposes the Free Movement Directive (Directive 2004/38/EC) into Irish law, orders can be made for both the removal and exclusion of citizens of the European Union, European Economic Area and Switzerland or their family members who represent a danger to public policy or public security. These orders can be made on the grounds of that the individual’s personal conduct represents a genuine, present and sufficiently serious threat affecting one of the fundamental interests of society. A removal order means the person must leave Ireland and if an exclusion order is made a re-entry ban can be imposed for a specified period, of up to ten years. The table below details the number of orders which have been enforced under the European Communities (Free Movement of Persons) Regulations 2015 from 2019 to 05 December 2025. Year 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025* Removal Orders Enforced 64 32 42 37 21 18 49 *(to 05/12/2025) * Please note, figures are correct at time of issue, however, all statistics may be subject to data cleansing. Information regarding the reasons for removal, the date on which each order was made and implemented, and whether a ten-year ban was applied in each case is recorded on each individual person’s file and is not available in a format which would readily allow detailed data to be extracted in the manner sought by the Deputy.

question: 606. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if the case of a person (details supplied) will be reviewed. [69316/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration As the Deputy will be aware, it is not the practice to comment publicly on individual cases. However, I can assure the Deputy that it is my policy to seek the removal of individuals from this State whose presence here is not conducive to the common good. When an EU citizen is convicted of a serious crime, they can be removed from Ireland in accordance with Directive 2004/38/EC, the “Free Movement Directive”. Removal orders can be made on the grounds that an individual’s personal conduct represents a genuine, present and sufficiently serious threat affecting one of the fundamental interests of society. Re-entry bans of up to 10 years can be applied to prevent their return to Ireland. Each case involves a detailed consideration to ensure the removal is appropriate and proportionate to the circumstances of the case. I can advise you that such removals are actively pursued by my Department and An Garda Síochána, who work closely to ensure high risk persons are prioritised and are removed from Ireland where possible.

question: 607. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the reason he announced recent significant changes to immigration policy at a press conference with the media, rather than on the floor of Dáil Éireann; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [69341/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can advise the Deputy that on the 26th of November I obtained government approval to introduce new policies and legislative changes to strengthen Ireland’s migration and asylum system to ensure it is rules-based, efficient and more aligned with EU Member States. These reforms also include a thorough review of the family reunification policy, developed with Minister of State Colm Brophy. These new policies and legislative changes are designed to strengthen the system integrity, enhance clarity for applicants, and ensure that migration pathways remain fair, transparent and sustainable. It is common practice for Ministers to signal forthcoming policy changes publicly once Government approval has been secured. This ensures wide public awareness and gives immediate clarity to applicants, practitioners, and other interested parties. Any matters that require changes to primary legislation will be subject to Oireachtas approval and debate in the normal manner.

question: 608. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 351 of 2 October 2025, if he is now in a position to provide an answer (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [69342/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration It is a central priority for me that Ireland’s immigration system is robust, and rules based. The enforcement aspects of our laws, including deportation orders, are an essential requirement for the system to work effectively and to ensure that there is confidence in the application of our legislation in this area. Deportations are costly and complex to enforce. It is the preferred option to return people voluntarily and my Department has a voluntary return programme to assist people to return prior to the issuance of a deportation order. A person can only avail of voluntary return before a deportation order is issued and I have increased resources into this programme to enable people who wish to return before a deportation order is issued to them. In 2024, 934 people left Ireland by way of voluntary return. This year 1,496 people have left Ireland by way of voluntary return up to 05 December 2025, which is an increase of 78% compared to the same period in 2024. A deportation order is a legal order to leave the State. If a person does not remove themselves from the State following the issuance of a deportation order, they will be removed, and my Department has taken action to significantly improve immigration enforcement measures and increase removals. The number of deportation orders signed in 2024 (2,403) increased by 180% compared to 2023 (857). This year 4,454 deportation orders have been signed up to 05 December 2025. So far in 2025, six charter flight operations have removed 205 people from the State. Of these, five operations to non-EU destinations removed 182 people who were subject to deportation orders and one operation removed 23 EU citizens on grounds of criminality. Any person who has been ordered to leave the State and fails to do so is committing a criminal offence, and can be arrested without warrant if they come into contact with An Garda Síochána. Such an order remains on the person’s record permanently, unless revoked by the Minister for Justice – it means they may not enter Ireland again in future. A person who is the subject of a deportation order may be detained for up to 56 days for the purpose of ensuring their deportation from the State. The prescribed places of detention for this purpose are contained in the Immigration Act 1999 (Deportation) Regulations 2005 and are: Castlerea Prison, Cloverhill Prison, Cork Prison, Limerick Prison, Midlands Prison, Mountjoy Prison, and Wheatfield Prison, as well as all Garda Síochána stations. However, not all of these locations are used for this purpose. I can advise the Deputy that of the 344 individuals whose deportation orders have been enforced by GNIB so far in 2025, 267 were detained prior to deportation. Of this group, 28 had criminal convictions. I can further advise that of the 267 people who were detained for the purposes of deportation this year up to 28 November, 206 were detained in Cloverhill Prison, 24 in Mountjoy Female Prison, 16 in Cork prison, 10 in Limerick prison, seven in Castlerea Prison, three in Midlands prison and one in Dublin Airport Garda Station. I have been advised by the Garda Commissioner that the number of people arrested in each year from 2020 - 2025 on foot of a deportation order is as follows: Year Number of people arrested on foot of a Deportation Order 2020 72 2021 <10 2022 31 2023 69 2024 159 2025 318* * (1) Year to date up to 24th October 2025 and (2) not all persons who are arrested on foot of a Deportation Order may be immediately removed due to legal or other logistical issues. ** During the COVID- 19 Pandemic there was a moratorium on deportations. This was effective during the latter part of 2020, 2021 and for the first 8 months of 2022. During the moratorium only persons who whose presence in Ireland would be contrary to the public interest were deported. This moratorium was lifted in July 2022.

question: 609. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 286 of 16 October 2025, if he is now in a position to provide the reply (details supplied); the reason a reply has not been forthcoming from Garda authorities; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [69343/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I refer to Parliamentary Question No. 286 of 16 October 2025 where you sought “the number of times An Garda Síochána have been deployed for protest management at Leinster House in 2024 and to date in 2025; the total expenditure incurred by An Garda Síochána for these deployments in both years; and if he will make a statement on the matter.” I am informed by the Garda authorities that, in 2024, Gardaí responded to 194 protest situations at Leinster House. 148 of these incidents required the deployment of approximately 5 Gardaí, 25 of these incidents required the deployment of approximately 10 Gardaí, and 21 of these incidents required the deployment of approximately 20 Gardaí. In total, 9,105 hours of policing were required at a cost of €364,200. In 2025, as of 28 November, Gardaí responded to 379 protest situations at Leinster House. 322 of these incidents required the deployment of approximately 5 Gardaí, 32 of these incidents required the deployment of approximately 10 Gardaí, and 25 of these incidents required the deployment of approximately 20 Gardaí. In total, 14,630 hours of policing were required at a cost of €585,200. The Garda authorities have advised me that total costs are based on an estimated overtime rate of approximately €40 per hour.

question: 610. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the amount spent on interpreters in the courts in each of the past five years; the name of each companies used; the breakdown of the amount paid to each company used, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [69358/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 586, 587, 588, 589, 610, 612, 613 and 615 together. The right to fair procedures is a central tenet of our criminal justice system. Ireland opted in to the EU Directive on the right to interpretation and translation in criminal proceedings and it was subsequently transposed into Irish law. This was done via two Statutory Instruments, one relating to Interpretation and Translation in Criminal Proceedings, which relates to the arrangements to be put in place by the Courts Service in respect of the conduct of court proceedings and the second which relates to Interpretation and Translation for Persons in Custody in Garda stations. Article 5 of the Directive reads that Member States are required to take ‘concrete measures’ to ensure the quality of the interpretation and translation services. A 2018 European Commission report on the implementation of Directive did not flag any issues of concern regarding Ireland’s approach to same and there are no open infringement proceedings underway in this regard. The manner in which these instruments are implemented in practice is an operational matter for An Garda Síochána and the Courts. The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána. I cannot intervene in operational Garda matters that fall under the Garda Commissioner’s remit, including the processes by which translation and interpretation services are provided. To be of assistance, I have requested the information sought in this regard from the Garda authorities. Regrettably, this was not available in time and I will write to the Deputy further once the information is to hand. Management of the courts and operational matters, including the management of interpretation services, are the responsibility of the Courts Service, which is independent in the exercising of its functions under the Courts Service Act 1998 and given the separation of powers in the Constitution. To be of assistance, I have referred the questions regarding costs and other operational matters to the Courts Service for direct reply.

question: 616. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding proposed changes to family reunification rules; if there is any impact on adult children of an essential worker who have already come to Ireland in recent years as permitted under previous family reunification rules; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [69372/25]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice I propose to take Questions Nos. 616 and 617 together. As the Deputy will be aware, on 26 November, I published the review of the non-EEA Family Reunification Policy, which has remained largely unchanged since 2013, and sets out how Irish citizens and most non-EEA Irish residents may apply to bring non-EEA family members to live with them in Ireland. The revised Policy includes a number of changes, the majority of which took effect for new applications from 26 November, with longer term measures to be introduced as soon as operational considerations allow. The revised policy can be accessed on my Department’s website at the following link: www.assets.gov.ie/static/documents/f88cb36e/Revised_Family_Reunification_Policy.pdf . As an outcome of this review, dependant minor children of Critical Skills Employment Permit, General Employment Permit and Intra-Corporate Transferee Irish Employment Permit holders, as well as Researchers on Hosting Agreements, who have been granted family reunification under the revised Policy, will now be registered on a Stamp 1G permission rather than a Stamp 3, upon reaching 16 years of age. This will allow the holder to take up employment without the need to obtain a separate Employment Permit of their own. For eligible dependant minor children already legally resident in the State with a Stamp 3 immigration permission, their permission will be varied to the same conditions as a Stamp 1G at their next online renewal. This also applies to people who were originally granted as a dependant minor child aged under 18 of their sponsor, as well as those aged 18 – 23 in full-time education, who were previously treated the same as dependant minor children under a derogation, which has now ended. The changes announced will therefore not have a negative effect on adult children previously granted family reunification. These arrangements do not apply to anyone who was a child over 18 years of age when they first received permission under the Non-EEA Family Reunification Policy, where it was under exceptional circumstances. Furthermore, under the revised Policy, and from 26 November 2025, applications for dependent minor children are only considered for children under the age of 18. Applications for adult dependent family members will be limited to parents and adult children with serious health conditions who cannot live independently. Income levels for sponsoring such dependent applications have been increased to €92,789 and will rise further each year. For any adult children over the age of 18 who wish to come to the State, it is possible to do so through the existing legal immigration pathways available. They can apply for a visa and for permission to remain in Ireland based on a variety of different reasons, including employment or education. Details of these legal pathways can be found on my Department's Immigration Service website here: www.irishimmigration.ie/ .

question: 620. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his Department intends to introduce a structured and standardised assessment of educational and professional qualifications for all residents in IPAS centres; the governance framework that would underpin such an assessment; the expected timelines for design and implementation; and the way the resulting data would support labour-market planning and policy oversight. [69561/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 591, 592, 593, 594, 595, 620, 621, 622, 623, 636, 637, 638 and 639 together. Applications for international protection are assessed as to whether the person in question has a well a well-founded fear for their safety in accordance with national, EU and international law. The education and qualifications held are not considered as part of this assessment. While immigration policy and operations are kept under constant review, there are no current plans to put in place an approach along the lines suggested by the Deputy. Labour market access permission for international protection applicants gives eligible applicants the opportunity to work and helps them to integrate into Irish society while providing for themselves and their families outside of the State’s directly provided services and supports. It also helps people to plan and prepare for their future in Ireland if they receive a positive decision on their application for international protection. Under the European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018 (S.I. No. 230 of 2018), people are eligible to apply for labour market access permission if: * They are an international protection applicant; and * They have waited at least 5 months from their “Application Received” date for their first instance recommendation; and * They are cooperating with the international protection process – delays in receiving a recommendation must not be attributable to the applicant. Following that, a person will be issued a permission for labour market access if, at 6 months, they have not yet received a first instance recommendation. This permission is valid for 12 months and may be renewed until a final decision is made on the person's international protection application. The table below shows the number of labour market access permission applications made and granted from 2018 to date. The granting of a labour market access permission does not necessarily confirm that the applicant has found employment. - Applications made Applications granted 2018 2886 1910 2019 2671 1794 2020 2799 2355 2021 4525 3985 2022 8807 6372 2023 13322 10101 2024 17078 16998 2025* 21140 19114 *2025 is correct as of 3 December 2025. It should be noted that labour market access for international protection applicants is not an alternative to a work permit; it is intended to allow certain applicants to work while they await a decision on their asylum application. This is to ensure that those found in need of protection can begin rebuilding their lives here. It is not intended as an alternative route to the established pathways for legal migration for the purposes of employment. The employment permits system is managed through the operation of the Critical Skills Occupations List and the Ineligible Occupations List which determine employments that are either in high demand or are ineligible for consideration for an employment permit. Further information on these can be found on the Department of Enterprise Trade and Employment's website below: [ Occupations Lists and SOC - DETE ] The Programme for Government 2025 provides a commitment to developing a new Migration and Integration Strategy for Ireland, detailing how we intend to meet the demands and the opportunities facing our society and economy over the next decade. This strategy is being led by my Department but will be a whole-of-Government Strategy intended to ensure our approach to migration is planned and coherent and balances the huge value of migrants in our economy and our society, while also ensuring that our rules are enforced. As part of the preparatory work for this strategy, my Department is identifying gaps in the existing research and data in relevant areas including on the fiscal and social dimensions of migration and integration in Ireland in support of the developing Strategy.

question: 623. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his Department’s data-governance policy regarding information collected from international protection applicants, including education, training, and work-history data submitted as part of permission-to-remain considerations; the reason this information is not recorded in a format that permits statistical analysis; and whether reforms to his Department’s data-architecture are planned to improve transparency and policy evaluation. [69564/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 591, 592, 593, 594, 595, 620, 621, 622, 623, 636, 637, 638 and 639 together. Applications for international protection are assessed as to whether the person in question has a well a well-founded fear for their safety in accordance with national, EU and international law. The education and qualifications held are not considered as part of this assessment. While immigration policy and operations are kept under constant review, there are no current plans to put in place an approach along the lines suggested by the Deputy. Labour market access permission for international protection applicants gives eligible applicants the opportunity to work and helps them to integrate into Irish society while providing for themselves and their families outside of the State’s directly provided services and supports. It also helps people to plan and prepare for their future in Ireland if they receive a positive decision on their application for international protection. Under the European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018 (S.I. No. 230 of 2018), people are eligible to apply for labour market access permission if: * They are an international protection applicant; and * They have waited at least 5 months from their “Application Received” date for their first instance recommendation; and * They are cooperating with the international protection process – delays in receiving a recommendation must not be attributable to the applicant. Following that, a person will be issued a permission for labour market access if, at 6 months, they have not yet received a first instance recommendation. This permission is valid for 12 months and may be renewed until a final decision is made on the person's international protection application. The table below shows the number of labour market access permission applications made and granted from 2018 to date. The granting of a labour market access permission does not necessarily confirm that the applicant has found employment. - Applications made Applications granted 2018 2886 1910 2019 2671 1794 2020 2799 2355 2021 4525 3985 2022 8807 6372 2023 13322 10101 2024 17078 16998 2025* 21140 19114 *2025 is correct as of 3 December 2025. It should be noted that labour market access for international protection applicants is not an alternative to a work permit; it is intended to allow certain applicants to work while they await a decision on their asylum application. This is to ensure that those found in need of protection can begin rebuilding their lives here. It is not intended as an alternative route to the established pathways for legal migration for the purposes of employment. The employment permits system is managed through the operation of the Critical Skills Occupations List and the Ineligible Occupations List which determine employments that are either in high demand or are ineligible for consideration for an employment permit. Further information on these can be found on the Department of Enterprise Trade and Employment's website below: [ Occupations Lists and SOC - DETE ] The Programme for Government 2025 provides a commitment to developing a new Migration and Integration Strategy for Ireland, detailing how we intend to meet the demands and the opportunities facing our society and economy over the next decade. This strategy is being led by my Department but will be a whole-of-Government Strategy intended to ensure our approach to migration is planned and coherent and balances the huge value of migrants in our economy and our society, while also ensuring that our rules are enforced. As part of the preparatory work for this strategy, my Department is identifying gaps in the existing research and data in relevant areas including on the fiscal and social dimensions of migration and integration in Ireland in support of the developing Strategy.

question: 624. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his Department’s policy for the collection, verification, retention and publication of incident data relating to International Protection Accommodation Services facilities; including the basis on which the Department determines what incident categories fall within its statutory responsibility; and what information is held for oversight and reporting purposes. [69568/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 624, 625, 626 and 627 together. The safety and wellbeing of all residents and staff in our accommodation centres is a priority for the Department and all International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) teams. IPAS is always available to deal with any complaints from residents and residents are encouraged to engage with IPAS if they are unhappy with any aspect of their accommodation. Where a complaint is significant in nature or a resident is not comfortable raising a complaint with a centre manager, they may make the complaint directly, or through a representative authorised to act on their behalf, to the IPAS Customer Service Team. Guidelines are in place for IPAS staff and Department officials in relation to responding quickly to any incidents, taking action to ensure people are safe. This includes reporting to An Garda Siochana if this is necessary. When any incident occurs, IPAS teams and centre management and staff work to ensure that residents involved can be supported, and that staff are trained and ready to respond in the right way, seeking support from officials and other agencies as needed. Staff and centre management are also equipped to support other people affected, including any family members or friends of the resident in the centre. Critical incidents are events that happen in a centre that are outside the normal range of experience and may lead to significant injury, property damage or even death. Incidents that arise in centres are defined and set out in IPAS policies, from a broad scale of general, minor incidents that include petty theft or damage to property, complaints about behaviour or noise, to include incidents considered critical in that they relate mental health or self-harm incidents, violence towards staff or residents, or the unexpected death of a resident. IPAS_Critical_Incident_Policy.pdf www.assets.gov.ie/static/documents/09fe3ad4/3._IPAS_Critical_Incident_Policy.pdf If a critical incident occurs in a centre, centre management will assess the situation and alert emergency services as appropriate. Critical incident staff training is provided to staff working in IPAS accommodation centres. They are given examples of what constitutes a critical incident and what to do to respond. Critical Incidents - 2025 (to end Oct 2025) Mental Health/self-harm 28 Violence towards staff/others 11 Deaths on-site 2 Other 20 Total 61 Information on the location of incidents is not reported in order to protect the privacy and confidentiality of resident information.

question: 628. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his Department carried out any risk assessments or safety audits of a facility (details supplied) between 1 January 2025 and 31 August 2025, and to provide the dates, scope and any non-operationally sensitive findings or recommendations arising from those assessments. [69572/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 628, 629, 630, 631, 632, 633, 673, 674, 675, 676, 677, 678, 679, 680, 681 and 682 together. In all International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) centres, whether they are commercially provided or State-owned, the accommodation service provider is responsible for the provision of services and is contractually obliged to ensure all activities at the property are within agreed standards and legal limits. Centre management and providers are responsible for day-to-day operational arrangements on the site, including staffing, catering, health and safety, utilities, security arrangements, and other requirements. This includes compliance with all child protection, safeguarding and other policies specified by IPAS as relevant to each centre and the services they provide, and set out in relevant legislation and regulations. Centres are subject to oversight arrangements and validation of compliance with all requirements through the Department's compliance team, with additional independent inspection and quality control through either Health Information and Quality Authority (HIQA) or IPAS-commissioned inspections. In relation to your questions about security services and procurement arrangements, the Department holds contracts with accommodation providers, who in turn are obliged to ensure provision of staffing and services at the centre. As such, the Department does not procure these services and therefore data is not available. In the accommodation contracts and appraisals carried out by my Department, in relation to security, requirements for security service provision are clearly set out, e.g. CCTV, 24 hour service, along with the need to comply with the licensing requirements of the Private Security Authority (PSA). In relation to reviews of security arrangements undertaken at Citywest during October and November 2025, my officials continue to work closely with An Garda Síochána to keep such arrangements under review. My Department does not disclose detailed information about security arrangements in this context.

question: 634. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his Department has assessed recent changes to naturalisation and settlement policies in the UK and other EU jurisdictions; if any analysis has been carried out regarding the potential implications of those changes for Ireland, including within the operation of the common travel area; if he will provide details of any ongoing or planned reviews of Ireland’s naturalisation procedures from an administrative and integration outcomes perspective; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [69579/25]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice Ireland and the United Kingdom share a long history and common interest in the effective operation of the Common Travel Area (CTA) and work together to prevent any abuses of the CTA. There is also significant operational cooperation between the Gardaí, UK Border Force, UK policing services and the Police Service of Northern Ireland in relation to both immigration and criminal matters. This strong practical engagement and cooperation serves the mutual interests of both Ireland and the UK, and will continue. The Government and I are acutely aware that changes to the UK’s immigration and asylum practices or laws can result in changes to the migratory flows between the UK and Ireland. We will closely monitor the changes proposed by the UK Government and if necessary, will respond to any changes made having considered them fully and discussed them with government colleagues. I can further advise the Deputy that last month Cabinet agreed to introduce new policies and legislative changes to strengthen Ireland’s migration and asylum system to ensure it is rules-based, efficient and more aligned with EU Member States. In these new policies I intend to make a number of changes to the rules on the granting of citizenship. The former policy of allowing individuals with international protection status to apply for citizenship after a time period of three years will no longer apply. In general, the time a successful international protection applicant must wait to apply for citizenship has now been extended from 3 to 5 years in line with most other citizenship applications. This came into effect from 8 December this year. I also propose to introduce additional eligibility criteria so that people seeking citizenship should be generally self-sufficient and should not owe a debt to the State for a defined period leading up to an application. Officials in my Department will work with the Attorney General’s Office and Department of Social Protection to develop this proposal. It is also proposed to exclude residency accrual for naturalisation purposes for those who are residing in Ireland on temporary permissions including Temporary Protection under the Temporary Protection Directive. This is simply intended as a clarification of existing policy which ensures that temporary permissions do not accrue reckonable residence in Ireland. Currently, there is an application fee of €175 and a certification fee of €950 following a positive decision. These fees will be reviewed in the context of ongoing efforts to modernise the system and the increased volume of applications being processed. I will also clearly define what constitutes “good character”, which often relates to criminal behaviour. This will clarify the application process for applicants, and the decision-making process for officials.

question: 635. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his attention has been drawn to concerns in relation to family court proceedings and the accessibility of Section 32 reports and related assessments (details supplied); if he will address these concerns to minimise delays in these proceedings; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [69585/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Under the provisions of the Courts Service Act 1998, management of the courts is the responsibility of the Courts Service, which is independent in exercising its functions. The conduct of court cases is furthermore a matter for the presiding judges, who are independent in the exercise of their judicial function, subject to only the Constitution and the law. It is not possible for me, as the Minister for Justice, to comment or intervene in any way in relation to how particular proceedings are conducted or on the outcome of those proceedings. As Minister for Justice, I am, however, committed to resourcing the courts sufficiently to ensure efficient and timely access to justice. As the Deputy is aware, section 32 of the Guardianship of Infants Act 1964 provides for the ordering of two types of report. Section 32(1)(a) allows the court to order a report, of its own motion or upon an application being made to it by a party to the proceedings, from an expert in writing on any question affecting the welfare of the child in proceedings concerning guardianship, custody or upbringing of, or access to a child. Section 32(1)(b) allows the court to order a report from an expert to determine and convey the child’s views in any proceedings related to guardianship of, custody of or access to a child. The sole purpose of the appointment of the expert under s.32(1)(b) is to express the wishes of the child either generally or in respect of specific questions on which the court may seek the child’s views. In both instances, experts are appointed by the Judge to compile a report for the Court’s consideration in the proceedings before it. Given the types of proceedings they relate to, such reports can contain very sensitive information on delicate matters, often relating to children. It is ultimately for the presiding judge to determine when, with whom and in what instances, if any, such reports should be shared.

question: 640. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he intends to introduce statutory safeguards governing the home delivery of alcohol, including requirements for delivery staff to refuse delivery where a person is visibly intoxicated or incapacitated; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [69612/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 640, 641, 642 and 643 together. The Programme for Government commits to updating our licensing laws. This commitment will be progressed in due course and public health will remain a key consideration for the Department throughout that process, in consultation with the Department of Health. Under existing legislation, where alcohol is purchased online, the same restrictions on the sale and supply of intoxicating liquor apply, including the restrictions in relation to hours of trading and the provisions in relation to the sale and supply of intoxicating liquor to young persons. Section 31 of the Intoxicating Liquor Act 1988, as amended, makes provision for offences relating to the sale and delivery of alcohol products to persons under the age of 18 years. It is an offence under section 31(2) for a licensee to sell or deliver, or to permit any other person to sell or deliver, alcohol products to any person for consumption off his or her licensed premises by a person under the age of 18 years in any place except with the explicit consent of the person's parent or guardian in a private residence in which he or she is present either as of right or with permission. On conviction for a first offence, a mandatory closure order of between two and seven days will be imposed by the court, together with a fine of up to €3,000. The penalties for a second or subsequent offence is a closure order of between seven and 30 days and a fine of up to €5,000. In addition, the licence holder is required to continue to pay staff for the duration of the closure period.

question: 651. Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration in relation to three asylum seekers who have been targeted for physical attack, if they will be moved to a new location to ensure that they are not targeted again given the circumstances (details supplied). [69673/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Government is determined to stamp out hate-motivated crimes and to protect vulnerable communities. The Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024 came into effect at the start of this year. The new legislation provides for increased prison sentences for certain crimes, where they are proven to be motivated by hatred, or where hatred is demonstrated based on the identity of the victims. I can assure the Deputy that An Garda Síochána takes hate crime very seriously. Every hate crime reported to An Garda Síochána is professionally investigated and victims supported during the criminal justice process. In relation to the Deputy's question about an IPAS centre and residents, the Department cannot comment on a matter that is part of a current criminal investigation. However, I can advise the Deputy that concerns about resident safety and welfare are treated as a priority. IPAS has a dedicated Resident Welfare Team who can provide supports to residents, and refer and connect them to specialist services as needed. They also have discretion to recommend a transfer of residents to alternative accommodation, where is this is considered necessary and where accommodation is available. Without breaching confidentiality of any resident, I confirm that my officials are aware of this case and are giving it attention.

question: 653. Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the specific legal or resource barrier that currently prevents the Department from mandating a four-week timeline for initial child contact assessments, mirroring the EU-based Danish family law system (Pillar 1); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [69702/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration As the Deputy will be aware, under the provisions of the Courts Service Act 1998, management of the courts is the responsibility of the Courts Service, which is independent in exercising its functions. The conduct of court cases is furthermore a matter for the presiding judges, who are independent in the exercise of their judicial function, subject to only the Constitution and the law. My Department is fully committed to reforming the family justice system in Ireland through implementation of the Family Justice Strategy 2022-2025. This is an ambitious programme of reform which sets out a vision for a system refocused on the needs and rights of children, who are central to many family justice matters. The Family Courts Act 2024 is a key component of my Department's Family Justice Strategy and contains a number of provisions designed to make the family court process more user-friendly and less costly. Commencing the Family Courts Act 2024 is a priority for Government and an implementation team has been established within my Department. As committed to in the Programme for Government, I intend to publish an implementation plan for a new Family Court System by the end of January 2026. The Act provides for the establishment of family court divisions within the existing court structures, namely a Family High Court, a Family Circuit Court and a Family District Court, each dealing with family law matters as appropriate to its jurisdiction. Each of these Family Courts will have judges with appropriate specialist knowledge assigned to them on a full-time basis, and the Act also provides for ongoing professional training in the area of family law. The Act includes a set of guiding principles for the family court system to make the best interests of the child a primary consideration in all family law proceedings, which all parties to proceedings will be required to have regard to. The principles include: • In family proceedings in which the welfare of a child is involved or likely to be affected, ensuring that the best interests of the child are a primary consideration; the child is informed in an age-appropriate manner; and the views of the child are ascertained and taken into account; and, there is no unreasonable delay in determining the proceedings. • The court placing an emphasis to minimise risk to the safety of any party to family law proceedings in cases where this is a concern. • Conducting proceedings in a manner which is user-friendly and accessible. • Encouraging and facilitating the use of alternative dispute resolution methods, such as mediation, to resolve family law disputes without recourse to the courts, in so far as is possible and appropriate. • Operating in an efficient manner which is likely to minimise the cost of the proceedings and encouraging active case management by the courts. Many families make their own arrangements in relation to access or contact. Where support is needed, this can be accessed initially via the range of universal and targeted parenting supports provided by the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality, the Child and Family Agency Tusla, and the network of family resource centres and other voluntary and community family support services which it funds. Where additional support is required, I am committed to facilitating the increased use of mediation, in line with the principles of the Family Courts Act 2024. Mediation offers people the opportunity to resolve their disputes without the adversarial strain of the courtroom. Goal 4 of the Family Justice Strategy aims to promote more co-operative, less adversarial ways for individuals, children and families to try to resolve disputes. This goal contains a number of actions relating to the role of mediation in family justice.

question: 654. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he is satisfied with the level of mental health support available for those seeking international protection upon arrival, particularly for those fleeing war zones and other highly traumatic situations; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [69709/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 654, 655, 656 and 657 together. I am very aware of the health and welfare needs of people applying for international protection, as by definition, many applicants are fleeing war and oppression in their home country. As such a range of assessments and services are provided to people, both on arrival and during their time in the process. These services are facilitated by IPAS teams and partners, and the HSE provides all substantive health and social cares services to people in Ireland, including IPAS residents. As set out in the reception conditions regulations, IPAS carries out Vulnerability Assessments for new arrivals, offered to single females, couples, and families who make an application for international protection and require accommodation from IPAS. The assessments are voluntary, and applicants are not required to participate or to share information with IPAS. Where an applicant participates and states that they, or their child, have a medical need or disability during an assessment, the person will be signposted to relevant services. Where appropriate, the applicant will be provided with information on how to make a self-referral or to directly access the relevant service. The information is also used by IPAS to appropriately accommodate people where required. Vulnerability Triage Assessments are offered to single male international protection applicants. The vulnerability triage aims to identify the most vulnerable within this group and ensure that they are prioritised for accommodation as soon as it is available. Once people are assigned accommodation, supports are provided to people and families staying in IPAS centres to access community services in relation to their physical and mental health, educational opportunities, and employment opportunities. The Health Service Executive (HSE) is responsible for providing health services in all communities, including people resident in International Protection Accommodation Service accommodation. Residents in IPAS accommodation centres are entitled to a medical card and access GP services within the local community. Specialist health and social care services for families are accessed through primary care, GP referral, and emergency services. In some larger IPAS Centres, in-reach medical or health care services may also be provided, through local arrangements with the health services in the area. If an international protection applicant or their child requires additional supports or if they develop a vulnerability during the application process, they may contact the Resident Welfare Team at IPAS at any time to seek support.

question: 658. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of gardaí who have been employed in the roads policing unit in each county, in each of the past ten years. [69717/25]

question: 665. Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will be prepared to seek a presidential pardon for the Catalpa Six ahead of next year’s 150th anniversary of the rescue; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [69759/25]

question: 669. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of those who entered the State as international students who have applied for asylum in 2025 and in each of the past five years, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [69785/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration It is a central priority for me that our international protection and immigration systems are robust and enforced. Under Section 15(1) of the International Protection Act 2015, a person who wishes to make a claim for international protection in Ireland must be at the frontier of the State or already be present in the State. The immigration history of individuals who apply for International Protection are noted as part of the application process; this will include information related to the manner in which they entered the State. While this information is recorded as part of an individual application for protection, this data is not managed in a format that would make it readily accessible. In preparation for the implementation for the EU Migration Pact in the second half of 2026, new arrangements for data collation and reporting are being put in place; this will include enhanced reporting capabilities in relation to matters such as prior immigration history.

question: 670. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the actions his Department is taking to establish a standardised and comprehensive data-recording framework for drone-related contraband incidents across the prison estate, including the development of specific incident classifications or codes for use by both the Irish Prison Service and An Garda Síochána, so that investigations, arrests, charges and convictions linked to drone incursions can be compiled and reported; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [69793/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 670 and 671 together. Preventing the access of contraband, including drugs, into prisons is a high priority for the Irish Prison Service, and it continues to examine technologies that might assist in making our prisons more secure, including anti-drone technologies. I am advised that the Irish Prison Service addresses drone incursions across the prison estate by deploying appropriate dynamic security measures responding to the nature and level of the threat in each instance. The controlled management of security-related information is a core component of maintaining a safe and secure custodial environment for staff, prisoners, and the wider community. There are no current plans to publish this information on an ongoing basis due to the risk of compromising the integrity, security, or safety of the prison estate. The Irish Prison Service, together with An Garda Síochána, have completed several very successful collaborative operations in the past year delivering significant results, including multiple arrests and prosecutions linked to attempts to introduce drugs and other contraband into prisons by drone or throw-over. This intelligence-led, multi-agency co-operation is effectively disrupting and detecting attempted delivery of contraband into prisons and improving communication pathways regarding supply, availability, typology and impact of illicit substances in prisons. In May of this year, the Irish Prison Service and An Garda Síochána signed a Memorandum of Understanding to formalise a framework for interagency cooperation. The Memorandum of Understanding was developed to enable the two organisations to work in partnership to prioritise cooperation in tackling organised crime, drug dealing and contraband smuggling. As the Deputy will be aware, the Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024. This includes all operational policing matters. Under Section 34(1) of the Policing Security and Community Safety Act 2024, the Garda Commissioner is independent in the performance of his functions.

question: 672. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if a formal written risk assessment on drone incursions into prisons is currently in place; the risk rating applied to drone-enabled contraband within the prison security framework; and if he will lay before Dáil Éireann a redacted summary setting out the main vulnerabilities identified, the mitigation measures underway, and the residual risks that remain outstanding. [69795/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I wish to inform the Deputy the Irish Prison Service does not disclose operational information that could compromise the integrity, security, or safety of any prison, or it’s environs. The controlled management of security-sensitive information is fundamental to maintaining a safe, secure, and orderly custodial environment for staff, prisoners, and the wider community. The release of such information could undermine established security protocols, expose potential vulnerabilities, or otherwise facilitate attempts to disrupt the safe operation of a prison. Accordingly, the Irish Prison Service adheres to a strict policy of withholding operational details from the public and will only release information that can be shared without compromising security, safety, or operational effectiveness.

question: 673. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the procurement basis on which security services have been engaged for a facility (details supplied) since 2021, including the legal rationale used to dispense with public tendering requirements under Directive 2014/24/EU and S.I. 284/2016. [69865/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 628, 629, 630, 631, 632, 633, 673, 674, 675, 676, 677, 678, 679, 680, 681 and 682 together. In all International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) centres, whether they are commercially provided or State-owned, the accommodation service provider is responsible for the provision of services and is contractually obliged to ensure all activities at the property are within agreed standards and legal limits. Centre management and providers are responsible for day-to-day operational arrangements on the site, including staffing, catering, health and safety, utilities, security arrangements, and other requirements. This includes compliance with all child protection, safeguarding and other policies specified by IPAS as relevant to each centre and the services they provide, and set out in relevant legislation and regulations. Centres are subject to oversight arrangements and validation of compliance with all requirements through the Department's compliance team, with additional independent inspection and quality control through either Health Information and Quality Authority (HIQA) or IPAS-commissioned inspections. In relation to your questions about security services and procurement arrangements, the Department holds contracts with accommodation providers, who in turn are obliged to ensure provision of staffing and services at the centre. As such, the Department does not procure these services and therefore data is not available. In the accommodation contracts and appraisals carried out by my Department, in relation to security, requirements for security service provision are clearly set out, e.g. CCTV, 24 hour service, along with the need to comply with the licensing requirements of the Private Security Authority (PSA). In relation to reviews of security arrangements undertaken at Citywest during October and November 2025, my officials continue to work closely with An Garda Síochána to keep such arrangements under review. My Department does not disclose detailed information about security arrangements in this context.

Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his Department’s procedures for ensuring that all personnel deployed at IPAS-managed accommodation centres hold valid licences issued by the Private Security Authority; and the way in which these compliance checks are monitored, recorded and enforced. [69869/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 628, 629, 630, 631, 632, 633, 673, 674, 675, 676, 677, 678, 679, 680, 681 and 682 together. In all International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) centres, whether they are commercially provided or State-owned, the accommodation service provider is responsible for the provision of services and is contractually obliged to ensure all activities at the property are within agreed standards and legal limits. Centre management and providers are responsible for day-to-day operational arrangements on the site, including staffing, catering, health and safety, utilities, security arrangements, and other requirements. This includes compliance with all child protection, safeguarding and other policies specified by IPAS as relevant to each centre and the services they provide, and set out in relevant legislation and regulations. Centres are subject to oversight arrangements and validation of compliance with all requirements through the Department's compliance team, with additional independent inspection and quality control through either Health Information and Quality Authority (HIQA) or IPAS-commissioned inspections. In relation to your questions about security services and procurement arrangements, the Department holds contracts with accommodation providers, who in turn are obliged to ensure provision of staffing and services at the centre. As such, the Department does not procure these services and therefore data is not available. In the accommodation contracts and appraisals carried out by my Department, in relation to security, requirements for security service provision are clearly set out, e.g. CCTV, 24 hour service, along with the need to comply with the licensing requirements of the Private Security Authority (PSA). In relation to reviews of security arrangements undertaken at Citywest during October and November 2025, my officials continue to work closely with An Garda Síochána to keep such arrangements under review. My Department does not disclose detailed information about security arrangements in this context.

question: 683. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the legal basis under which his Department intends to introduce accommodation charges for applicants for international protection residing in IPAS centres; if a regulatory impact assessment has been carried out; and if he will publish the legal advice underpinning the proposed changes. [69929/25]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 683, 684, 685 and 686 together. The 2025 Programme for Government includes a commitment to introducing a contribution model for people in international protection accommodation. Proposals for residents to make a contribution to the cost of international protection accommodation were considered by Government and are now being progressed by the Department. The contribution to cost scheme will be implemented within a planned 12-month period, allowing for the development of systems and resources to assess eligibility, share data securely and collect and process payments. IPAS Accommodation is provided for in EU regulations and transposed into Irish law. Statutory Instrument No 230/2018, European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018, provides that all IP applicants are entitled to Material Reception Conditions. This is defined as housing, food and associated benefits provided in kind, the daily expenses allowance (DEA), and clothing provided by way of financial allowance under section 201 of the Social Welfare Consolidation Act 2005. DEA is currently set at €38.80 per week per adult and €29.80 per week per child. Because of the specific legal status of people applying to for international protection, during their application process they do not have access to standard social welfare benefits, nor to standard housing services and entitlements. As such, any State accommodation which is provided to them as part of material reception conditions is not private rented accommodation and is subject to the above regulations instead. The Regulations further provide, at section 5, that where a resident is in receipt of an income above a certain level, they may be required to make a contribution to the cost of providing reception condition services. The contribution rates are set out in a Schedule to the Regulations and are proportionate to the amount that people earn, as set out below. question: 687. Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to the recommendation included in the European Commission's 2025 Rule of Law Report for Ireland (details supplied), the steps being taken to address this recommendation; the expected timeline for the completion of same; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [69986/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration In July of this year, I obtained Government approval to prepare a General Scheme of a Civil Reform Bill. The Civil Reform Bill is a key implementation measure of the Kelly Report of the Review of the Administration of Civil Justice. As part of the Bill, it is my intention to introduce provisions which will codify the existing law on judicial review by placing it on a statutory basis. The measures should achieve greater transparency in the law and lead to a more streamlined review process. Key reforms should ensure that the system cannot be misused on purely technical grounds, costs are reduced where possible and litigants have sufficient standing to properly challenge decisions. The Civil Reform Bill will also contain measures to reform the law on: • Discovery and production of documents; • case conduct principles for civil litigation; • presumption against adjournments; • deemed discontinuance of actions; • creation of a standard claim notice; • monetary jurisdictions of the courts in civil matters; and • other aspects of the Kelly Review. These reforms are aimed at addressing costly bottlenecks in the legal system and delivering a more efficient, fair, accessible and lower cost system of civil litigation. Further and in-depth discussions will take place as part of the pre-legislation scrutiny process of the Civil Reform Bill, where stakeholder views will be sought. While the Kelly Review made recommendations on measures to address the costs of litigation, it failed to reach a consensus on one primary approach to regulate them. Instead, two options were put forward: a set of non-binding guidelines; and the development of a table of maximum costs. In the absence of a clear primary recommendation in this area, the Minister requested that research be commissioned on the options set out in the Review. To evaluate the matter further, the Department commissioned Indecon Economic Consultants to undertake a multi-criteria analysis of the two approaches set out in the Review Report. The Department also asked Indecon to consider other models that may achieve the goal of controlling litigation costs. The Report identified four possible models to control litigation costs but identified a dearth of data in relation to legal costs in Ireland. One of the options examined was that of providing a scale of fees for legal costs. Such an option has been provided for in the Planning and Development Act, and my Department is liaising with the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment around the development of scales of fees for Judicial Review applicants in the the context of commencing that Act. It is hoped that the outcome of that project can then be extended to other areas of litigation.

question: 688. Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to a recommendation (details supplied) included in the European Commission's 2025 Rule of Law Report for Ireland, the steps taken to address this recommendation; the expected timeline for the completion of same; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [69989/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Programme for Government commits to pass the Defamation (Amendment) Bill to balance freedom of expression with protections for individuals’ good name and reputation, which includes safeguards against SLAPP suits (strategic lawsuits against public participation) to prevent misuse of defamation laws to stifle public interest reporting. As the Deputy will be aware, the Bill was passed by Dáil Éireann on 2 July 2025. Committee Stage of the Bill in Seanad Éireann commenced on 17 July 2025 and will resume for the 9th time on 11 December. The Bill provides for a range of reforms to address concerns raised during the public consultation on the review of the Defamation Act 2009. These include provisions to enhance protection for responsible public-interest journalism and public participation. The Bill provides for an amended and simplified defence for publication in the public interest. It introduces safeguards to prevent abusive proceedings against public participation (SLAPPs) in defamation cases, including early dismissal, security for costs and the ability for targets of SLAPP proceedings to seek declarations, more generous costs orders and damages. The safeguards provided for transpose key requirements of the EU Anti-SLAPP Directive with respect to defamation proceedings. The Bill also provides for the abolition of juries in High Court defamation cases, which is expected to significantly reduce delays, legal costs, the length of hearings, the unpredictability of outcomes and the incidence of disproportionate damages. It should also ensure greater clarity on the law and reduce the need for expensive appeals because judges, unlike juries, will be required to provide reasons for decisions. This is an important Bill that balances and safeguards the rights to freedom of expression with the protection of a person's good name and reputation, and the right of access to justice. It will bring much needed reform to defamation law and the priority remains to proceed to enactment as soon as possible.

question: 689. Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when an application will be processed and an IRP card issued to a person (details supplied) given it is over eight weeks since the application was submitted; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [70008/25]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The application referred to by the Deputy continues to be processed by my Department. The Registration Office within Immigration Service Delivery of my Department provide a live processing date, which is updated every Monday, and is available at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/renewing-your-registration-permission-if-you-live-in-the-republic-of-ireland/#processing They are currently processing applications submitted from 10 October 2025. In order to ensure a fair and equitable service, renewals are processed in order of date submitted. If the application is approved, the person concerned can expect to receive their new Irish Residence Permit (IRP) card within the following 10-15 working days. I can advise the Deputy that my Department has put in place arrangements for people awaiting a renewal of their IRP card who are travelling over the Christmas period. Details are available at link: www.irishimmigration.ie/isd-announces-initiative-to-facilitate-customers-travelling-at-christmas-2/ The person concerned can now directly check the status of their immigration application on the Immigration Service’s new Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at [ portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/ ]. As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 696. Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration with regard to the Kilbride Army camp which is being used as an IPAS centre, if he is aware that enhanced safety measures are required as a result of recent attacks on men; if he will consider transferring them to a safe place; if swift action will be taken to ensure their continued protection; if an investigation will be carried out into the threats and harassment they are facing when they leave the camp; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [70034/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Government is determined to stamp out hate-motivated crimes and to protect vulnerable communities. The Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024 came into effect at the start of this year. The new legislation provides for increased prison sentences for certain crimes, where they are proven to be motivated by hatred, or where hatred is demonstrated based on the identity of the victims. I can assure the Deputy that An Garda Síochána takes hate crime very seriously. Every hate crime reported to An Garda Síochána is professionally investigated and victims supported during the criminal justice process. In relation to the Deputy's question about an IPAS centre and residents, the Department cannot comment on a matter that is part of a current criminal investigation. However, I can advise the Deputy that concerns about resident safety and welfare are treated as a priority. IPAS has a dedicated Resident Welfare Team who can provide supports to residents, and refer and connect them to specialist services as needed. They also have discretion to recommend a transfer of residents to alternative accommodation, where this is considered necessary and where accommodation is available. Without breaching confidentiality of any resident, I confirm that my officials are aware of this case and are giving it attention.

question: 701. Deputy Alan Kelly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the way in which he is ensuring that the collection and exchange of biometric data is carried out in compliance with domestic and international human rights law. [70090/25]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Biometric data is collected for a range of criminal justice and immigration management purposes. Biometric data is collected by the Irish Immigration Service and the International Protection Office and agencies and statutory bodies under the aegis of my Department including An Garda Síochána and Forensic Science Ireland. The collection and storage of such data is subject to appropriate safeguards and is underpinned in all cases by relevant legislation to permit the collection and sharing of such data. The data collected is stored in a number of databases such as the Automated Fingerprint Identification System (AFIS) and the Garda National Immigration Bureau Information System (GNIB-IS) or the National DNA Database System. The key piece of domestic legislation that provides for the taking of biometric samples is the Criminal Justice (Forensic Evidence and DNA Database System) Act 2014, which sets out in law the strict procedural guidelines with regard to the collection, transfer and retention of biometric data. There are long-standing sharing arrangements in place with international policing and security partners. Access to the national DNA database and automated fingerprint information system by other States is strictly controlled and has regard to data protection requirements in respect of personal data. In this regard privacy rights are protected in accordance with the EU General Data Protection Regulation, 2016/679 (GDPR), the EU Law Enforcement Directive 2016/680 (LED) and the Data Protection and the Data Protection Act 2018. Securing and managing personal data in accordance with the GDPR principles is a priority and is governed by a comprehensive set of policies, procedures and systems. My Department has implemented appropriate measures to ensure that all data held under its control is secure and is not at risk from unauthorised access. Measures for the protection of personal data are reviewed and upgraded where appropriate, on an ongoing basis. Insofar as DNA is concerned, the DNA Database System Oversight Committee oversees the management and operation of the DNA Database System for the purposes of maintaining the integrity and security of the System and for that purpose to satisfy itself that the provisions of the 2014 Act in relation to the System are being complied with. The Committee is independently chaired by Justice Catherine Murphy.
